content: Progestin-only oral contraceptives are prescribed to prevent pregnancy. Progestin is a synthetic form of the female hormone progesterone. It works by inhibiting ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries), altering the cervical mucus to make it more difficult for sperm to reach the egg, and modifying the uterine lining to prevent implantation of a fertilized egg. These contraceptives are highly effective in preventing pregnancy but do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV/AIDS. Progestin-only oral contraceptives are available as tablets taken orally. They must be taken once daily, at the same time every day. It is essential to follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully. If you have any questions, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Take the medication exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency. Each pack contains 28 pills, and you should start the next pack immediately after finishing the previous one. Ideally, begin taking the pills on the first day of your menstrual period. If you start on another day, use a backup method of contraception (e.g., condoms or spermicide) for the next 48 hours. If you have had a miscarriage or abortion, you can start taking the pills the following day. Progestin-only contraceptives are safe for breastfeeding mothers. Fully breastfeeding mothers (exclusively breastfeeding without formula or other foods) can start the medication six weeks postpartum, while partially breastfeeding mothers should begin three weeks postpartum. Before starting this medication, request and carefully read the manufacturer’s patient information leaflet from your doctor or pharmacist. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before taking progestin-only oral contraceptives, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to progestins, aspirin, tartrazine (a yellow food dye), or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention medications such as carbamazepine (Tegretol), phenobarbital (Luminal, Solfoton), phenytoin (Dilantin), and rifampin (Rifadin), as these may interact with progestin-only contraceptives. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have or have ever had breast lumps, breast cancer, abnormal vaginal bleeding, liver tumors, liver disease, or diabetes. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or if you become pregnant while taking this medication. If you use tobacco products, inform your doctor, as smoking increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Avoid smoking while taking this medication. Unless otherwise instructed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember and continue taking the pills at your regular time. If you are more than three hours late taking a dose, use a backup method of contraception for the next 48 hours. If you are unsure about missed doses, continue taking the pills and use a backup method until you consult your doctor. Progestin-only oral contraceptives may cause side effects. Mild side effects include irregular menstrual periods, headaches, breast pain, upset stomach, dizziness, acne, and increased hair growth. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, though uncommon, include prolonged bleeding, absence of menstrual periods, and severe stomach pain. Combined estrogen and progestin contraceptives are associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer, and liver tumors, but it is unclear if progestin-only contraceptives carry the same risks. Discuss the potential risks with your doctor. Report any unusual problems or side effects to your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly. Consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Inform laboratory personnel that you are taking progestin-only oral contraceptives, as they may interfere with certain tests. Rarely, women may become pregnant while taking oral contraceptives. If it has been more than 45 days since your last period, or if your period is late and you missed doses or took them late while having unprotected sex, take a pregnancy test. If you wish to become pregnant, stop taking the medication. Progestin-only contraceptives should not delay your ability to conceive. Do not share this medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
